Subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs (p95/p99) - Hosted API vs Current Provider

Thanks again for the call today — really helpful to walk through the architecture and the tradeoffs. Quick recap from our side and a couple of asks so we can qualify next steps: 

- Our primary goal: 95th/99th percentile end-to-end latency (p95/p99) for customer-facing chat where typical prompts are ~200 tokens and responses average ~300 tokens.
- Current baseline from our provider (VendorX): p95 ~650ms, p99 ~1.8s for short prompts (200 tokens) under our normal traffic profile.
- Target we need for production: p95 <= 400ms, p99 <= 800ms for >=95% of traffic. Streaming is required for UI behavior (token-by-token) with low time-to-first-byte (<150ms p95).
- Concurrency: typical concurrent sessions ~120, peak bursts up to ~600 concurrent in a short window. Throughput target: sustained ~100 req/s, burst to 300 req/s.

Immediate asks:
1) Can Redwood hosted API hit p95/p99 targets for our observed prompt/response size and concurrency?
2) How would you recommend we configure batching/streaming to meet the TTFB requirement?
3) We'll share a small test dataset and synthetic load profile if you can set up a short PoC to compare hosted vs our current provider.

Attaching call notes and the current VendorX latency export. Would appreciate a short reply confirming what Redwood needs to run a side-by-side test.

Best,
Alex

Alex — thanks for sharing the numbers. A few notes from the performance team after a quick pass: 

Short answers up-front: yes, we expect Redwood Hosted to meet the targets in most cases with the right config. We'll need to validate with your exact payloads and the real end-to-end measurement points you use.

Details / assumptions (please confirm):
- Model family and size: assuming 7B-class optimized quantized model for chat (if you're using much larger models that will change latency). Confirm what model your product uses.
- Prompt/response lengths: your average sizes (200/300) align with our initial tests. Our hosted baseline for similar 7B quantized models and typical network paths: p95 ~220–320ms, p99 ~550–750ms end-to-end for single-request streaming (TTFB p95 ~90–140ms), at 100 req/s sustained with 128 concurrency.
- For bursts to 300 req/s and concurrency ~600 we recommend: request-level autoscaling + a short-lived burst tier, and enabling continuous batching up to ~64 tokens per microbatch for throughput efficiency. That typically keeps p95 within target while lowering cost.

Streaming specifics:
- We stream token-by-token with an initial TTFB that depends primarily on scheduling and first decode (~60–120ms typical internal). Over the public internet add ~20–50ms depending on regions.
- To meet p95 TTFB <150ms we recommend: 1) pin to nearest region, 2) use our streaming endpoint (not multipart), and 3) enable lightweight prefix caching if you have repeated prompts.

Measurement plan (PoC):
1) Redwood will run a side-by-side against VendorX using your synthetic load (we will mirror your frontend measurement points so p95/p99 are end-to-end comparable).
2) We'll provide a CSV with per-request timings (time-to-first-byte, per-token gaps, token count, end-to-end).
3) Deliverable: summary dashboard (p50/p95/p99 for TTFB and end-to-end), raw CSV, config recommendations (batching, quant profile, instance sizing).

Open question: can you confirm whether you can obfuscate the test prompts (so we can run in a shared test tenancy) or if this must run in a dedicated VPC? If dedicated, we can discuss a short Dedicated trial.

Next steps: Laura to schedule the PoC kickoff, Alex to share artifacts.

—Marissa
Performance Lead, Redwood Inference
